title: 01. Fundamentals & Trade-offs: Functional Requirements vs Non-Functional Requirements
summary: Functional requirements (FRs) describe what a system must do (features, behaviors, inputs, outputs); non-functional requirements (NFRs) describe how the system must behave while doing it (scalability, availability, latency,…

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Functional requirements (FRs) describe **what** a system must do (features, behaviors, inputs, outputs); non-functional requirements (NFRs) describe **how** the system must behave while doing it (scalability, availability, latency, security, usability).

Every system design conversation starts with requirements gathering, and the single most common mistake candidates make is conflating the two kinds. A functional requirement is a statement of behavior the system must exhibit: "a user can upload a profile picture up to 5 MB," "the system must shorten a URL and return a 7-character code," "the API must return the current balance for an account." Functional requirements are testable with assertions: you can write a unit test that calls the endpoint and checks the response. They define the contract — the inputs, the outputs, the state changes — and they are usually the things product managers obsess about. When you list APIs and data models, you are listing functional requirements made concrete.

Non-functional requirements are different in kind. They are qualities of the system, not behaviors. "The shorten endpoint must respond in under 50 ms at p99," "the service must be available 99.99% of the time," "the system must scale to 10K QPS," "user passwords must be stored using bcrypt with cost factor 12," "the API must be usable from a screen reader." None of these is a single behavior; they are constraints on every behavior. NFRs are testable too, but the tests are different — load tests, chaos tests, security audits, accessibility audits. They are also typically the things that get cut first when schedules slip, which is why they must be written down and tracked explicitly. The acronym **USARI** (Usability, Availability, Scalability, Reliability, Integrity) is a useful checklist; others add Performance, Maintainability, Compliance, and Observability. The exact acronym matters less than the habit of asking "and what else?" until you have at least five NFRs on the wall.

Why does the distinction matter in practice? Because the design decisions for FRs and NFRs are made by different people at different times and have different costs. FRs are owned by product and engineering together and change weekly. NFRs are owned by platform, SRE, and security and tend to be stable over years. An FR is "easy" to add late — ship a new endpoint. An NFR added late is brutal: retrofitting 99.99% availability onto a system designed for 99% requires multi-region failover, and retrofitting sub-50 ms latency onto a chatty synchronous service requires a rewrite. Good designers extract NFRs aggressively up front because they are the constraints that actually shape the architecture. If you do not know your latency budget, you cannot decide between a synchronous RPC and an async event. If you do not know your availability target, you cannot decide between single-region and multi-region. If you do not know your retention requirement, you cannot size storage.

Real-world example: Netflix publishes its NFRs explicitly. The playback service targets **99.99% availability** (about 52 minutes of downtime per year) and **<100 ms playback startup latency** at p95 globally. Those two NFRs cascade through the entire architecture. The availability target forces a multi-region active-active deployment on AWS, with each region able to serve all traffic if the other fails. The latency target forces a CDN-first design (Open Connect appliances inside ISP networks) so that the first video segment is served from a box physically near the user, not from a regional origin. The latency target also forces aggressive pre-fetching of manifests and the first few segments when a user hovers over a title. None of these architectural decisions follow from the FR ("user can play a movie"); they all follow from the NFRs. Strip away the NFRs and you would design a very different, much cheaper, much worse system.

Another real-world example, this time from Amazon: the FR of the checkout button is "charge the customer and create an order." The NFRs around it are ferocious — payment authorization must never double-charge even if a network call times out (consistency/integrity), the checkout flow must stay up during Prime Day traffic spikes 100x above baseline (scalability/availability), and the entire flow must be auditable for PCI compliance for 7 years (integrity/compliance). Those NFRs are why Amazon runs an idempotent, event-sourced checkout pipeline with saga-pattern distributed transactions rather than a simple synchronous charge call.

A common pitfall in interviews is jumping to architecture before NFRs are stated. The candidate hears "design a URL shortener" and immediately draws a load balancer and Cassandra. The right move is to ask: "What QPS do we expect? What latency? What availability? What retention? Is analytics a concern?" Those five questions often reshape the entire design — a 10 QPS internal tool can be a single Flask app on a laptop, while a 100K QPS public service needs sharding, caching, and a CDN. Another pitfall is writing NFRs that are not measurable — "the system should be fast" is not an NFR; "p99 latency < 200 ms for the top 5 endpoints" is.

FRs and NFRs connect to every later phase of this curriculum. Scalability (Topic 3) is an NFR. Availability (Topic 4) is an NFR. Latency budgets drive caching strategy (Phase 4) and load-balancing policy (Phase 5). Security and integrity drive Phase 10. Observability NFRs drive Phase 11. When you cannot decide between two architectures, the tie-breaker is almost always an NFR you have not yet written down — go back and elicit it.

### ASCII Diagram
```

   ----------------             ------------------------
   - shorten URL                - <50 ms p99 latency
   - return 7-char code         - 99.99% availability
   - redirect on visit          - 10K QPS read, 100 QPS write

            |    Sharded DB)   |
            +-------------------+
```

### Walkthrough
1. Elicit functional requirements first — list the APIs, the data model, and the user-visible behaviors. Make them testable.
2. Elicit non-functional requirements explicitly using a checklist (USARI: Usability, Availability, Scalability, Reliability, Integrity). Make each one measurable with a number.
3. Cross-check: every architectural component must trace back to at least one FR or NFR; every NFR must have an owner and a test. Components with no justification get deleted; NFRs with no test get redefined.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# A toy requirements parser that classifies a sentence as
# Functional (FR) or Non-Functional (NFR), and tags the NFR
# category using a USARI checklist. Illustrates the kind of
# heuristic a PM tool might run on a backlog of tickets.

import re

NFR_KEYWORDS = {
    "Usability":   ["usable", "accessible", "wcag", "screen reader",
                    "i18n", "localized", "responsive"],
    "Availability":["availability", "uptime", "sla", "failover",
                    "redundan", "99.9", "99.99", "99.999"],
    "Scalability": ["scale", "throughput", "qps", "rps", "concurrent",
                    "users per", "requests per", "horizontal", "shard"],
    "Reliability": ["reliab", "durable", "consistent", "idempotent",
                    "at-least-once", "exactly-once", "retry", "mtbf"],
    "Integrity":   ["secure", "encrypt", "audit", "compliance",
                    "gdpr", "pci", "pii", "tamper", "auth"],
    # cross-cutting
    "Performance": ["latency", "p99", "p95", "ms", "response time",
                    "budget", "slowness"],
}

FR_VERBS = ["shall", "must", "should", "can", "allows", "enables",
            "supports", "provides", "returns", "creates", "uploads",
            "downloads", "sends", "receives", "displays", "stores"]

def classify(text: str) -> dict:
    t = text.lower()

    # Step 1: look for NFR keywords first; they are more specific.
    matched = []
    for cat, kws in NFR_KEYWORDS.items():
        for kw in kws:
            if kw in t:
                matched.append((cat, kw))

    # Step 2: detect numeric thresholds — strong NFR signal.
    has_number = bool(re.search(r"\b\d+(\.\d+)?\s*(ms|s|%|qps|rps|gb|tb|mb)\b", t))

    # Step 3: FR heuristic — has a behavior verb and no NFR signal.
    has_fr_verb = any(v in t for v in FR_VERBS)

    if matched or has_number:
        kind = "NFR"
        primary = matched[0][0] if matched else "Performance"
        evidence = matched[0][1] if matched else "numeric threshold"
    elif has_fr_verb:
        kind = "FR"
        primary = "behavior"
        evidence = "behavioral verb"
    else:
        kind = "UNCLEAR"
        primary = "?"
        evidence = "no signal"

    return {
        "text": text,
        "kind": kind,
        "category": primary,
        "evidence": evidence,
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    samples = [
        "User shall be able to upload a profile picture up to 5MB.",
        "The shorten endpoint must respond in under 50ms at p99.",
        "The service must be available 99.99% of the time measured monthly.",
        "The system must scale to 10000 QPS sustained.",
        "Payments must be idempotent — no double-charge on retry.",
        "User can shorten a URL and receive a 7-character code.",
        "The UI must be WCAG AA accessible.",
        "Click analytics must be retained for 5 years for audit.",
    ]
    for s in samples:
        r = classify(s)
        print(f"[{r['kind']:6}] ({r['category']:12}) {s}")
        print(f"        evidence: {r['evidence']}")
```
